baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Canadian imperialism read as one form of Canadian nationalism, through the ideas of its leading spokesmen (1970)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3). Of the earlier critics he writes that 'When critics belaboured imperialism because of its hostility to “Canadian nationalism” what they really meant was that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed. There have been many varieties of Canadian nationalism'; imperialism was 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission' (p. 9). His method: 'inquiring into the ideas and ideals which men in the past read into their interpretations of Canada and by exploring the relationship between these conceptions and the environment in which they circulated' (p. 10). The conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). In-period reception. Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, pp. 274–276, read in full): the book's 'grande originalité' is to conclude that the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (p. 275); the book is 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' (p. 276). Monet also reports the first criticisms (p. 275 and nn. 2–4): neglect of the economic and military sides of imperialism (Robert Page, JCS 1970), the folding into a Canadianizing ideology of witnesses 'qui seraient plutôt des représentants du pan-britannisme' (Douglas Cole, JCS 1970), and too much weight on 'une petite élite' of intellectuals (H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum 1970); Page, Cole (1970) and Nelles are not read here. Cole's 1971 comparative article (notes read; body closed) says that Berger 'makes the strongest case for a Canadian nationalistic consciousness within these terms' (n. 33). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979, read): he 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists', but 'Their nationalism and their imperialism were, however, decidedly masculine affairs' (p. 10); intellectual history 'will have to take women into account' (p. 10). Clarence Karr (1989, re-read): Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' (p. 161); 'Carl Berger's critics accuse him of an over-Canadianization of imperialism and of ignoring a broader Anglo-Saxon perspective in what Graham Carr refers to as a “scavenger hunt for nationalism”' (pp. 162–163); since his book, group biography 'has been upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method of addressing the Canadian intellectual tradition' (p. 167), and its premise that imperialism can 'only be understood in relation to the characters who espoused it and who came to personify it' risks making thought 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe' (p. 168). Carr's article (JCS 1982) is checked at its journal abstract only. A contribution, not an origin: Monet credits Penlington with the suggestion. Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Doug Owram's introduction to the 2013 edition (snippet view) calls it 'pretty much the standard interpretation of the way in which Canadian nationalism evolved' (p. xi).

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: The liberal nationalist account of imperialism as a colonial past defeated by Canadian nationalism, criticised (1970)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The interpretation he set out to revise: 'The conflict between imperialism and nationalism added up to a struggle between the past and the future, the desire to remain a colony and the wish to be a free nation. Once this framework was accepted, it was easy to account for the failure of imperialism: it succumbed to Canadian nationalism. The main outlines of this interpretation survived largely because of the great influence of O. D. Skelton's biography of Laurier and because of the long dominance of a particular school of Canadian historiography of which it was the finest expression. This so-called liberal nationalist school has lately come under some penetrating scrutiny, its insufficiencies have been exposed and its continued relevance questioned. Naturally, its interpretation of imperialism has also been found wanting, at least by implication' (p. 9). Against it he argued that critics who attacked imperialism for 'its hostility to “Canadian nationalism”' 'really meant that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed' (p. 9). In-period corroboration that this was the received English-Canadian view: Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, read in full) writes that the imperialists 'ont eu très mauvaise presse parmi les historiens du Canada' and that English-Canadian historians, 'partisans pour la plupart de l'explication de l'équipe gagnante', saw them as 'des conservateurs retardataires' (p. 274); Berger 'vient maintenant nuancer ces jugements... téméraires' (p. 274). The same judgement runs into his historiography: in The Writing of Canadian History (1976) the main criticism of English-Canadian historians, as Allen Mills reads it (1977, read), is that they wrote 'as if they were contributing to pressing matters of contemporary public concern, especially the matter of national survival' (Mills's words, pp. 135–136). A counter-critique: Graham Carr (JCS 1982; journal abstract only) argues that 'revisionists such as Carl Berger, while ostensibly challenging Whig assumptions about imperialism/nationalism, actually share many of the traditional views'. The arrow records Berger's criticism of a position, the liberal nationalist account of imperialism; it does not claim that the national-tradition historians shared one view, and Skelton, whom he names, has no atlas entry.

relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Miville (2016) compares Creighton and Brunet as public intellectuals: both denounced official bilingualism, Creighton to defend Macdonald's founding vision, Brunet because the country was built by two nations. The Centenary Series translated Trudel (1973) and Ouellet (1980) into the English national synthesis; Berger's subtitle restricts his analysis to English-Canadian writing. Comparison, not influence. PhD context: 68 of 173 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Laurentian & national tradition also engage the Quebec historiography anchor set (39% vs 16% of all; lift 2.51). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Brunet’s ‘English presence’ and ‘two Canadas’ (1958 subtitle) and the Laurentian national tradition are parallel national historiographies with different subjects and politics. Title-level.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Ideas and representations of Canadian nationhood
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Berger's chapters on Canada First and "The Canadian Character"; Vance on war memory and Canadian nationalism; Igartua on the shift from ethnic to civic national identity. Comparison: the Canadian works rarely engage the modernist theory debates of the atlas entry in the checked pages.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Historical writing treated as a domain of English-Canadian intellectual history and its national preoccupation examined (1971–86)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Trofimenkoff (1979, p. 9, read): 'some of the people have suggested that the leit motiv of both English and French Canadian historical writing, in itself a domain of intellectual history, has been the concern for survival, a nationalist concern'; her note 4 cites Ramsay Cook's essays 'La Survivance French Canadian Style' and 'La Survivance English Canadian Style' in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 114–40, 141–65; not read here). Karr (1989, p. 161, read) places Berger's analysis of 'the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote' among the English-Canadian intellectual historians' studies of nationalism. Berger's 1986 chapter records that 'J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261, snippet view). The arrow records intellectual historians making the national tradition's writing an object of study; Berger's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (the Canadian persons Tier 1 revision).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: English-Canadian and Quebec histories of ideas and commemoration
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Lamonde's histoire sociale des idées is Quebec's counterpart; Nelles studies Quebec's tercentenary and Coates and Morgan Madeleine de Verchères. PhD context: 16 of 27 PhDs citing Lamonde (2000) are at francophone universities, against 2 of 48 for Berger (1976).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Careless's second thoughts about the 'flood' of regional, cultural and class writing (1979 lecture) read as a reaction reasserting 'a "positive" unifying national history' (1988); a decade earlier the working-class bibliography Kealey co-compiled had invoked Careless's limited identities (1973)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Kealey's words, in period. Introduction to Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (St. John's: CCLH, 1988; reprint of a Canadian Journal of Sociology special issue), pp. 1–7, read in the AU Press PDF: 'The degree to which reaction has re-emerged to reassert the need for a "positive" unifying national history can be seen by contrasting the views of J.M.S. Careless in 1969 and in 1980. In 1969, Careless enthusiastically embraced Ramsay Cook's earlier call for the study of region, class, and ethnicity … By 1980, however, he had serious doubts' (p. 2); he quotes Careless's farmer 'in the midst of the flood' and answers: 'As I hope this volume suggests, such plaintiff [sic] Toronto cries to date have not been able to dam the flood of critical scholarship on class, gender, and region' (p. 3). 'The impatience mentioned by Berger and articulated by Careless addresses itself as much to this regional revolt as it does to writings concerned with class and gender' (p. 5). Careless's text, re-read (Manitoba History no. 1, web text, unpaginated; the 1979 Jackson lecture, cited by Kealey as 1980): 'there has been a massive outpouring … on class disparities and stresses and such things as national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted. In this situation, I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood'. Qualifications kept: Careless continues, 'there are reasons why I do not really feel as bad as the foregoing might suggest', calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' of the study of limited identities, and asks that class identities 'be treated in their national scope', a point close to Kealey's own (1981, p. 77). Kealey's 'reaction' is his reading of the lecture. Earlier connection: Careless (1979) quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History (1973, p. 11), compiled by Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Warrian: 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada'. Kealey (1981, p. 68) says that statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. No reply by Careless was checked. Related: edge_954 (Careless → who_killed_debate) records the fragmentation worry this passage voices; pe138_kealey_rel_02 records Kealey's separate critique of limited identities from a class standpoint (1978).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Bederman credits Higginbotham’s analysis of race and gender among recent theoretical discussions informing the intersection she investigates.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: At5 Bederman explicitly adopts Hazel Carby’s call to interrogate racial specificity and whiteness. Note23 also identifies Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, together with Berger/Brown/Hewitt and Lerner, as important recent theoretical discussions. This plural, bounded historiographic resource does not replace the more direct Carby credit or imply exclusive derivation. Higginbotham original unread; no guessed correction of the date as printed in Bederman’s note.
